text.content:
Storyteller-only spoiler content. The Week of Nightmares is a scripted, canon, Gehenna-adjacent crossover event: the Ravnos Antediluvian awakens, fights, dies, and its death-curse triggers a clan-wide fratricidal massacre among the Ravnos. Running it requires the Storyteller to know the whole shape of events in advance so she can seed foreshadowing and manage pacing — none of this should be looked up by players. Official World of Darkness chronology places it in Bangladesh in July 1999, though a Storyteller is free to retime it to fit her own chronicle.

What Actually Happens (Offstage, Ground Zero)

The Ravnos Antediluvian (called Churka or Ravanna) awakens in Pakistan, drawn by the blood of its childer and grandchilder spilled in earlier battles with the Cathayans, and immediately slakes an ancient thirst on nearby Methuselahs of its own line. Three Cathayan bodhisattvas recognize the danger and move to intercept it. On the third night the Antediluvian and the three bodhisattvas meet in open battle in Bangladesh: one Cathayan summons a hurricane as both weapon and sun-shield so the fight can continue into the day, another weakens the Gauntlet and calls spirits to the fight, and thousands of Bangladeshis die in the resulting flooding. The Technocracy declares Code Ragnarok, brings solar-reflector satellites to bear, fights the storm with techno-magical aircraft, and finally drops Hellstorm neutron bombs on the battlefield. The nuclear detonations kill the three bodhisattvas and everyone else nearby, but also weaken the Antediluvian enough that when the clouds part, four suns' worth of reflected sunlight finally destroys it, early on the fourth night.

Before it dies, the Antediluvian's final act is to curse all of its childer: a broadcast command driving every Ravnos, worldwide, regardless of sect, blood bond, Vaulderie, or torpor, into an overwhelming cannibalistic bloodlust that makes them attack any other Ravnos on sight. Over the following three nights the Ravnos slaughter each other; the curse then fades, leaving only confusion, suspicion, and perhaps a hundred Ravnos left alive worldwide — none of them elders.

Global Psychic Fallout (All Vampires)

Because the awakening and death of an Antediluvian is a mystical event of planetary scale, every vampire (and much of the mortal world) feels reverberations regardless of proximity to Bangladesh:

  • Nights One and Two: Everyone is edgy and short-tempered from unremembered nightmares. At the Storyteller's discretion, this can be played as pure roleplaying color (more Virtue Tests called for), or mechanically enforced by giving every character the Nightmares Flaw (a one-Trait penalty on all challenges) for the duration — in which case consider also requiring a minimum two-Trait bid on challenges so the stakes of losing escalate along with everyone's frustration.
  • Visions: Any character with an Oracular Ability Merit or three or more derangements experiences involuntary visions of the Antediluvian's awakening and its call to its childer. Escaping a vision costs one Willpower Trait, and even then the respite lasts only one scene. Auspex grants no special insight into these events, and Malkavian insanity provides no particular edge in interpreting them — they are as in the dark as anyone else. The thaumaturgical Path of Spirit Manipulation may surface some information from spirits, but it will be as confusing as anyone else's visions; a Storyteller may also rule that any ritual capable of shedding real light on events takes so long to prepare that the Week is over before it completes.
  • The Third Night specifically: Same edginess for most characters as Nights One-Two. All Ravnos, however, gain three extra levels of Chimerstry for the duration of the battle, which may exceed their normal generational limits. The Storyteller may assign a bonus or penalty of one to five Traits to any use of Chimerstry each scene to reflect the battle's shifting fortunes. All Ravnos also suffer a one-Trait penalty on Virtue Tests, and a Ravnos who frenzies during this night may use any Chimerstry power without spending Willpower.
  • Nights Four through Seven (post-Antediluvian-death): The edginess and visions fade for everyone else, but the Ravnos curse activates. Each Ravnos must win a Self-Control/Instinct Static Challenge or fall into a cannibalistic frenzy whenever she awakens and whenever she encounters another Ravnos — no disguise or ignorance of the other vampire's clan grants immunity; the Blood simply knows. Difficulty scales by generation: two Traits for 12th generation or lower (i.e., higher-numbered/younger), three Traits for 8th–11th generation, four Traits for 7th generation or higher (older). This is not a one-time test; it recurs at every waking and every Ravnos encounter until the curse lifts.

The Sole Survivor

The section header refers to the practical, near-universal outcome of the Week of Nightmares for any city with more than one Ravnos: by the end of the week, at most one will be left alive, and it is entirely possible none survive. The book does not present this as a formal elimination-tournament subsystem beyond the frenzy/Self-Control mechanic above — the Static Challenge above, repeated at every encounter between Ravnos, is the actual mechanism that grinds the clan down. A solitary Ravnos in a city with no clanmates nearby only has to contend with the unnatural hunger itself (and the temptation to go looking for kin), but the moment two Ravnos meet, the challenge above is made and, on a loss, a fight to the death (frequently ending in diablerie) follows.

A Ravnos who survives is not in the clear afterward. Consequences to plan for:

  • She may face a blood hunt or Sabbat pack retaliation for whatever she did in frenzy, including breaches of the Masquerade or diablerie of a clanmate (which other Kindred can sometimes detect by sight, especially if it happened during frenzy).
  • The clan's traditional protection — harassing a lone Ravnos usually drew reprisal from the rest of the clan — is effectively gone, leaving survivors exposed to old grudges and general opportunism.
  • A possible upside: a Ravnos who diablerized a clanmate during the frenzied binge may have lowered her generation, though with almost no elders left to teach higher Chimerstry, that benefit is hard to cash in. Reduced Ravnos numbers may also open up Roma herd territory, though many Roma become leery of anyone claiming Ravnos heritage, and the near-extinction of the clan grants remaining Ravnos a strange kind of anonymity: almost no one expects to meet one anymore.

Storyteller Procedure: Running the Event

Deciding Whether to Use It

Consider the chronicle's current arc before dropping this in: it works best either as a fresh complication when a prior story arc has just wrapped, or as a deliberate reminder that the setting is a World of Darkness, not just a City of Darkness. Avoid using it to steal the spotlight from a player's ongoing plan, though intentionally deflating an overconfident character's hubris is a legitimate use. Avoid introducing it during a period of unrelated chaos unless deliberate pandemonium is the goal.

Scaling Local Impact

How hard a given city feels the Week of Nightmares depends on what's already in the chronicle: a city with no Ravnos, no active oracles, and no one listening to the local asylum's ravings can pass through with only generalized edginess and bickering (though the long-term fallout still applies). A city with a Ravnos enclave, a chantry of Noddist scholars, and an attentive Malkavian primogen will feel it very directly. Track four channels of exposure: (1) the Ravnos themselves, who are the real stars of the local drama; (2) spontaneous visions among the psychically sensitive (oracular Kindred, the institutionalized, occasionally ordinary-seeming people); (3) Allies/Contacts/Mentors/Influence reporting odd developments — higher Influence ratings (5+) warrant more detailed, more alarming intelligence, while ratings of 4 and below only pick up local color, and different Influence categories (Occult, Health, Church, Media, Street) naturally produce more relevant leads than others (Bureaucracy, Finance); and (4) the mundane media, which the Masquerade keeps vague and buried (a stray mention of a typhoon over India, a human-interest piece about an artist's sudden obsession with a Ten-Headed God), with small-press, alternative and internet sources occasionally carrying more accurate fragments.

Delivering Information to Players

Decide whether to tell each character privately that she feels anxious for no reason (encourages a paranoid, someone's-out-to-get-me read) or to tell the whole troupe at once that something citywide is amiss (skips straight to a shared mystery). If an oracular character is in a public space like Elysium when a vision hits, everyone present notices something is wrong even without knowing what; if only the institutionalized are affected, only Malkavians checking in on their kin are likely to learn anything early. As with any information the Storyteller controls, tune the pacing and accuracy of what leaks out to serve the story rather than to be strictly fair.

Handling Ravnos Player Character Deaths

With multiple Ravnos in a chronicle, character death is close to guaranteed for all but one. The Storyteller has several non-exclusive options for softening or dramatizing this:

  • Let the cards fall where they may: Treat it like any other character loss with no special cushioning — suitable for players who don't mind rolling a new character or who see their characters as subordinate to the story.
  • Ravnos Death Match: Warn the Ravnos players in advance that only one will survive, turning it into an openly competitive storyline. Only appropriate for players who can handle direct antagonism toward each other without it souring the table.
  • The Dramatic Exit: Recruit a player to actively stage-manage her own character's demise as a memorable set-piece, potentially leaving complications for her surviving comrades to deal with.
  • The Consolation Prize: Offer a player who accepts a scripted death some compensation for her next character (e.g., approval for a concept she'd wanted but hadn't been allowed) — use sparingly, since it sets a precedent other player deaths may be expected to match.
  • The Plant: If the chronicle is short on Ravnos, or the Storyteller wants a larger body count for dramatic effect, introduce Storyteller- or Narrator-controlled Ravnos NPCs specifically to participate in and be consumed by the event, taking care that their disposable nature isn't obvious to the players.

The Storyteller should also decide up front how much foreshadowing to give affected players: telling a player outright that Final Death is likely in the next session or two, keeping it entirely secret and managing the fallout after the fact, or delivering a smaller, personal vision (distinct from the setting-wide Antediluvian visions) that only makes sense in hindsight once the Week is underway.

Long-Term Aftermath (Epilogue Events)

Rumors filter in from other cities as communications allow, diverging over time into urban legend (entertaining but unreliable), each sect's official story (self-justifying and reassuring to the rank and file), and rare carefully-researched truth. The Camarilla's default response is denial — acknowledging an Antediluvian awakening is doctrinally too close to Sabbat belief, so princes suppress or explain away the evidence, and anyone caught insisting otherwise risks correction or an archon's visit. The Sabbat, conversely, treats it as vindication ("the Antediluvians are real, we were right"), though factional infighting over who should lead the response continues regardless. The independent clans (surviving Ravnos, Assamites, Gangrel, Giovanni, Followers of Set) each have their own stake in learning the truth and protecting themselves; the Followers of Set in particular may try to profit by trading information, accurate or not. Expect a spike in demand for lore, forgotten Book of Nod fragments, and self-styled experts (real or charlatan), and expect surviving Ravnos to face backlash as their diminished numbers become common knowledge — treated by different princes/bishops as pariahs, scapegoats, useful curiosities, or (rarely) refugees worth protecting. The event is also a natural moment for existing or newly-formed Gehenna cults to become active, recruiting or studying anyone touched by the visions or the few Ravnos survivors; new cults formed in direct response to the Week tend to be unsubtle and short-lived, and are prime targets for infiltration by either sect.
